questions.q: In the `AIClientWrapper` class, what is `self.history` used for?
options: It stores the class's documentation string
It tracks every prompt sent through this particular instance, across multiple calls to ask()
It's a required argument to __init__ with no other purpose
It stores the wrapper's own source code
questions.explain: self.history starts as an empty list in __init__, and each call to ask() appends to it — giving the object memory of its own past activity, which a plain function couldn't maintain without a global variable.

questions.q: Why does `ask()` return an `AIResponse` dataclass instance instead of just a plain string?
options: A dataclass runs measurably faster than returning a string
Python requires every method to return a dataclass
It keeps the door open for more structured fields (like token counts) later, without breaking code that already uses response.text
Strings cannot be returned from instance methods
questions.explain: A structured return value can grow new fields over time while existing calling code (which only reads response.text) keeps working unchanged — the same reasoning real SDK response objects follow.

questions.q: What would have to change in the code that CALLS `client.ask(prompt)` when Chapter 5 swaps the mocked reply for a real `requests.post()` call inside `ask()`?
options: Every single call site across the whole program would need rewriting
Nothing — the public shape (construct with api_key, call ask(), get an AIResponse back) stays the same; only the one line inside ask() changes
The class would need a completely different name
AIClientWrapper would need to become a dataclass itself
questions.explain: Because the wrapper's public interface doesn't depend on how ask() gets its answer internally, swapping the mocked line for a real HTTP call only touches that one method body — calling code is unaffected.

questions.q: What does the leading underscore in a method name like `_headers` conventionally signal in Python?
options: That the method is internal / not part of the class's intended public interface, though it's still technically callable
That the method is automatically private and cannot be called from outside the class
That the method must be called before __init__
That the method only works with integers
questions.explain: A single leading underscore is a naming convention, not an enforced restriction — it signals to other developers that a name is an internal implementation detail, even though Python doesn't actually block access to it.

questions.q: Why does each `AIClientWrapper` instance have its own independent `history` list rather than sharing one across all instances?
options: Because `history = []` is declared inside `__init__`, making it an instance attribute set fresh (via self) for every new object
Because Python automatically shares all list attributes across instances
Because `history` was declared as a class attribute outside `__init__`
It doesn't — all instances actually do share the same history list
questions.explain: Lesson 13 covered this distinction: attributes assigned with self.x inside __init__ are instance attributes, created fresh per object, unlike a class attribute defined directly under the class body which would be shared.
